hints: Focus on the lone pair on the ligand and which particle supplies both electrons for the bond to the metal.
walkthrough:
Picture the bond as a gift of electrons**
Think of a transition metal ion like $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ as electron deficient with empty orbitals ready to accept electrons. A ligand is simply the partner that brings the electrons. The key idea is that both electrons in the bond come from the same side, from the ligand.

Lock in the exact definition**
That type of bond where the ligand supplies both bonding electrons is called a dative covalent or coordinate bond. So a ligand is defined as any molecule or ion that forms a dative bond to a central metal atom or ion. Since $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ is bidentate, one ion forms two such bonds using two lone pairs.
Final answer: A ligand is a species that donates a lone pair of electrons to a central metal atom or ion to form a dative (coordinate) bond.

hints: Count the coordination number from two bidentate $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ plus two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and recall the octahedral arrangement around $\text{Cr}$.
Think where the two identical monodentate $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands can sit relative to each other, next to each other at 90 degrees or opposite each other at 180 degrees.
walkthrough:
Work out the shape you are drawing in**
Chromium is surrounded by two $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ ions each bonding twice plus two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecules bonding once. That is $2 \times 2 + 2 = 6$ bonds, so coordination number 6, octahedral. The template shows $\text{Cr}$ with six octahedral directions. Each bidentate oxalate must span two neighbouring, cis positions because it is too short to span across the metal.

Draw the trans isomer first**
Put the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands opposite each other, for example one on the top vertical bond and one on the bottom vertical bond (180 degrees apart). Then place one $\text{O-O}$ oxalate chelate on the left side linking the left dashed and solid wedge bonds, and the second $\text{O-O}$ oxalate on the right side linking the right dashed and solid wedge bonds. This is the trans diaqua form.

Draw the cis isomer**
Now put the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands next to each other, for example one on the top vertical bond and one on one wedge bond in the plane (90 degrees apart). Fill the remaining four octahedral positions with the two $\text{O-O}$ oxalate groups, each joining two adjacent positions. This is the cis diaqua form, non superimposable on the trans form, so they are stereoisomers (cis-trans isomers).

Final answer: cis-$[\text{Cr}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_2(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2]^-$: the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands are adjacent (90 degrees to each other).
trans-$[\text{Cr}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_2(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2]^-$: the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands are opposite (180 degrees to each other, trans across Cr). Each $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ occupies two cis positions.

hints: Write the dissolution equilibrium for solid $\text{CaC}_2\text{O}_4$ breaking into its aqueous ions and remember which species are omitted from equilibrium constants.
Recall how units are built from the units of concentration ($\text{mol dm}^{-3}$) raised to the power of each concentration term in the expression.
walkthrough:
Write the dissolving equilibrium**
Solid calcium ethanedioate dissolves like this:
$$\text{CaC}_2\text{O}_4(\text{s}) \rightleftharpoons \text{Ca}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + \text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}(\text{aq})$$
$K_{sp}$ is just the equilibrium constant for this sparingly soluble salt dissolving.

Build the expression correctly**
For equilibrium constants you include aqueous concentrations but never include solids because their concentration is constant. With 1:1 stoichiometry there are no powers:
$$K_{sp} = [\text{Ca}^{2+}][\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}]$$
Each concentration has units $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$, and multiplying two together gives $\text{mol}^2 \text{dm}^{-6}$.

hints: Convert the given solubility from $\text{g dm}^{-3}$ to $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ using $M_r$ of $\text{CaC}_2\text{O}_4$.
Use the 1:1 dissolving ratio to link the molar solubility to $[\text{Ca}^{2+}]$ and $[\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}]$ before substituting into the $K_{sp}$ expression.
walkthrough:
Convert grams to moles**
$K_{sp}$ needs concentrations in $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$, but you are given $6.65 \times 10^{-3} \text{ g dm}^{-3}$. Calculate $M_r$:
$$M_r = 40.1 + 2(12.0) + 4(16.0) = 128.1$$
Then:
$$\text{solubility} = \frac{6.65 \times 10^{-3}}{128.1} = 5.19 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$
This is the moles of $\text{CaC}_2\text{O}_4$ that dissolve per $\text{dm}^3$.

Square the solubility to get Ksp**
Each mole that dissolves gives one $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and one $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$:
$$[\text{Ca}^{2+}] = [\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}] = 5.19 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$
Substitute:
$$K_{sp} = (5.19 \times 10^{-5})^2 = 2.69 \times 10^{-9}$$
Rounded to two significant figures in standard form:
$$K_{sp} = 2.7 \times 10^{-9} \text{ mol}^2 \text{dm}^{-6}$$

Final answer: $M_r(\text{CaC}_2\text{O}_4) = 128.1$
solubility $= 6.65 \times 10^{-3} / 128.1 = 5.19 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol dm}^{-3} = [\text{Ca}^{2+}] = [\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}]$
$K_{sp} = (5.19 \times 10^{-5})^2 = 2.7 \times 10^{-9} \text{ mol}^2 \text{dm}^{-6}$
